concepts.name: Emotional abandonment
concepts.note: An emotional state in which people feel undesired, left behind, insecure, or discarded.

concepts.name: Separation anxiety
concepts.note: A fear response triggered by a threat or disconnect within a primary attachment.

concepts.name: Primal abandonment fear
concepts.note: The feeling experienced when left alone without anyone to care for one's needs.

concepts.name: Autophobia
concepts.note: A specific phobia of isolation, or a morbid fear of being alone or isolated.

methods.name: Acceptance and commitment therapy
methods.note: A therapy that focuses on avoiding painful emotions and memories while accepting uncomfortable thoughts and feelings.

concepts.name: Acceptance
concepts.note: Recognition and assent to the finality of a situation without attempting to change or protest it.

concepts.name: Self-acceptance
concepts.note: The state of being satisfied with one's current self, or the ongoing process of striving for that satisfaction.

concepts.name: Social acceptance
concepts.note: Being included in a group, formally or informally, without being judged or disapproved of by others.

concepts.name: Public acceptance
concepts.note: A general agreement.

concepts.name: Cultural acceptance
concepts.note: Respecting people for their culture, traditions, clothing, or appearance without judging them.

concepts.name: Conditional acceptance
concepts.note: Acceptance that requires modification of initial conditions before final acceptance.

concepts.name: Expressed acceptance
concepts.note: An overt and unambiguous acceptance of set conditions.

coined_terms.name: Acceptance and commitment therapy
coined_terms.note: Developed by Steven C. Hayes in the 1980s.

concepts.name: Psychological flexibility
concepts.note: The capacity developed through ACT's core processes to respond effectively to experience and act according to values.

concepts.name: Self-as-context
concepts.note: A transcendent, observing sense of self distinct from one's thoughts, feelings, sensations, and memories.

concepts.name: Observing Self
concepts.note: A consistent perspective from which to observe and experience private events.

concepts.name: Cognitive defusion
concepts.note: Reducing the tendency to reify thoughts, images, emotions, and memories.

principles.name: Acceptance
principles.note: Allowing unwanted private experiences to come and go without struggling with them.

principles.name: Contact with the present moment
principles.note: Awareness of the here and now with openness, interest, and receptiveness.

principles.name: The observing self
principles.note: Accessing a transcendent sense of self with an unchanging continuity of consciousness.

principles.name: Values
principles.note: Discovering what is most important to oneself.

principles.name: Committed action
principles.note: Setting goals according to values and carrying them out responsibly.

methods.name: Mindfulness
methods.note: Recognizing psychological responses and being open to and accepting one's experiences.

frameworks.name: Six core principles
frameworks.note: ACT's six principles for developing psychological flexibility: defusion, acceptance, present-moment contact, observing self, values, and committed action.

concepts.name: Accountability
concepts.note: Acknowledgment and assumption of responsibility for actions, products, decisions, and policies.

concepts.name: Account-giving relationship
concepts.note: A relationship in which one party must inform another about actions and decisions, justify them, and face punishment for misconduct.

concepts.name: Political accountability
concepts.note: A condition in which citizens can reward or sanction politicians for choices made on their behalf.

frameworks.name: Accountability modes
frameworks.note: Forms of accountability identified in the scientific literature, including administrative, judicial, market, political, professional, and social accountability.

concepts.name: Agency
concepts.note: The capacity of an actor to act in a given environment.

concepts.name: Human agency
concepts.note: The claim that humans make decisions and enact them in the world.

concepts.name: Moral agency
concepts.note: Agency as it pertains to questions of moral responsibility.

concepts.name: Sense of agency
concepts.note: The feeling of ownership or control.

concepts.name: Individual agency
concepts.note: Individual choices and the ability to influence one's life conditions and chances.

concepts.name: Collective agency
concepts.note: Pooling knowledge, skills, and resources to act in concert and shape the future.

concepts.name: Everyday agency
concepts.note: Agency expressed through consumer and daily choices.

concepts.name: Strategic agency
concepts.note: The capacity to affect wider system change.

principles.name: Principle of rationality
principles.note: The view that context-sensitive, goal-directed efficient actions are crucial characteristics of agents.

theories.name: Action theory
theories.note: The philosophical discipline concerned with studying agency.

theories.name: Reciprocal causation
theories.note: The view that people make causal contributions to their own motivations and actions.

frameworks.name: Agency and structure
frameworks.note: The enduring debate between individual capacity to act and social factors that limit or influence opportunities.

concepts.name: Appraisal
concepts.note: An evaluation or estimate of an event that causes a specific emotional reaction.

concepts.name: Structural approach
concepts.note: An approach explaining appraisal of emotions through the structure of appraisal.

concepts.name: Process model
concepts.note: A model explaining how emotions can develop through appraisal processes.

concepts.name: Physiological arousal
concepts.note: A physiological component discussed in relation to whether emotions can occur without it.

theories.name: Appraisal theory
theories.note: The theory that emotions are extracted from evaluations of events.

theories.name: Appraisal theories of emotion
theories.note: Theories stating that emotions result from interpretations and explanations of circumstances, even without physiological arousal.

concepts.name: Arete
concepts.note: A concept in ancient Greek thought referring to excellence of any kind and realization of potential or inherent function.

concepts.name: Moral virtue
concepts.note: Excellence understood specifically as virtue.

concepts.name: Praxidikai
concepts.note: Arete and Homonoia collectively, meaning “Exacters of Justice”.

concepts.name: Paideia
concepts.note: The ancient Greek training of a boy to manhood.

coined_terms.name: Secure base
coined_terms.note: Introduced by Mary Ainsworth in the 1960s and 1970s; an attachment figure from which a child explores and to which the child returns for comfort.

concepts.name: Attachment
concepts.note: An affectional bond or tie between an individual and an attachment figure.

concepts.name: Internal working models
concepts.note: Patterns formed through caregiver interactions that influence future relationships.

concepts.name: Separation anxiety
concepts.note: A normal and adaptive response for an attached infant following loss of an attachment figure.

axioms.name: Set-goal
axioms.note: For infants and toddlers, the hypothesized goal of maintaining or achieving proximity to attachment figures.

theories.name: Attachment theory
theories.note: A psychological and evolutionary theory concerning human relationships and the importance of early bonds.

theories.name: Object relations theory
theories.note: One of the theories whose concepts Bowlby's theory integrated.

theories.name: Control systems theory
theories.note: One of the theories whose concepts Bowlby's theory integrated.

frameworks.name: Attachment patterns
frameworks.note: The patterns identified in infants: secure, avoidant, anxious, and disorganized attachment.

coined_terms.name: Perceived locus of causality
coined_terms.note: Introduced by Fritz Heider to define the perception of the causes of one's environment.

concepts.name: Attribution
concepts.note: A perceived cause of an everyday experience, understood as external or internal.

concepts.name: External attribution
concepts.note: Interpreting behavior as caused by the individual's environment.

concepts.name: Internal attribution
concepts.note: Assigning the cause of behavior to an internal characteristic such as ability, personality, mood, or motivation.

concepts.name: Fundamental attribution error
concepts.note: The tendency to favor dispositional or personality-based explanations over external factors.

concepts.name: Culture bias
concepts.note: Assuming something about behavior based on one's own cultural practices and beliefs.

concepts.name: Self-serving bias
concepts.note: Attributing success to internal factors and failure to external, uncontrollable factors.

concepts.name: Defensive attribution hypothesis
concepts.note: A social-psychological term for a set of beliefs held about attribution.

theories.name: Attribution theory
theories.note: A theory explaining how individuals perceive the causes of everyday experience.

theories.name: Covariation model
theories.note: The model that attributes behavior to factors present when behavior occurs and absent when it does not.

theories.name: Theory of self-determination
theories.note: A theory influenced by perceived locus of causality that uses it to measure feelings of autonomy.

frameworks.name: Three-dimensional model
frameworks.note: Bernard Weiner's model organized around stability, locus of causality, and controllability.

frameworks.name: Achievement attribution
frameworks.note: Weiner's attribution framework with stability, locus of causality, and controllability categories.

concepts.name: belief revision
concepts.note: The process of changing beliefs to take into account a new piece of information.

concepts.name: update
concepts.note: Changing old beliefs to take account of a change when new information concerns the present and old beliefs concern the past.

concepts.name: revision
concepts.note: Adding new information about the same situation while avoiding inconsistency.

concepts.name: contraction
concepts.note: Removal of a belief.

concepts.name: expansion
concepts.note: Addition of a belief without checking consistency.

concepts.name: extraction
concepts.note: Extracting a consistent set of beliefs and/or an epistemic entrenchment ordering.

concepts.name: consolidation
concepts.note: Restoring consistency of a set of beliefs.

concepts.name: merging
concepts.note: Fusing two or more belief sets while maintaining consistency.

axioms.name: AGM postulates
axioms.note: Properties that a revision operator should satisfy to be considered rational; named after Alchourrón, Gärdenfors, and Makinson.

principles.name: minimal change
principles.note: The knowledge before and after change should be as similar as possible.

concepts.name: intrinsic cognitive load
concepts.note: The effort associated with a specific topic.

concepts.name: germane cognitive load
concepts.note: The work put into creating a permanent store of knowledge, or schema.

concepts.name: extraneous cognitive load
concepts.note: The load arising from the way information or tasks are presented.

concepts.name: schema
concepts.note: The primary unit of analysis used in cognitive load theory for designing instructional materials.

concepts.name: working memory
concepts.note: A limited cognitive resource whose concurrent load constrains learning.

theories.name: cognitive load theory
theories.note: John Sweller's theory guiding presentation of information to optimize intellectual performance by accounting for working-memory limitations.

theories.name: information processing theory
theories.note: A theory whose aspects cognitive load theory uses to emphasize limitations of concurrent working-memory load.

frameworks.name: three types of cognitive load
frameworks.note: The distinction among intrinsic, extraneous, and germane cognitive load.

concepts.name: cognitive reframing
concepts.note: Identifying and changing how situations, experiences, events, ideas, and emotions are viewed.

concepts.name: expressive suppression
concepts.note: Holding back or hiding an emotion after it has already arisen.

concepts.name: cognitive distortion
concepts.note: An exaggerated, typically negative thought unsupported by a rational thought process.

methods.name: cognitive restructuring
methods.note: A therapeutic tool for changing a person's mindset.

methods.name: cognitive reappraisal
methods.note: A strategy that changes how a situation is understood before an emotional reaction fully develops.

frameworks.name: process model of emotion regulation
frameworks.note: James Gross's model in which reappraisal operates early, before an emotional reaction has fully developed.

concepts.name: compliance
concepts.note: A submission or response made in reaction to a request.

concepts.name: social influence
concepts.note: The effect of other people's words, actions, or presence on thoughts, feelings, attitudes, or behavior.

concepts.name: informative social influence
concepts.note: Influence pursued to achieve accuracy.

concepts.name: normative social influence
concepts.note: Influence pursued to achieve affiliation and social approval.

principles.name: Strength
principles.note: The stronger or more important a group is to an individual, the more likely compliance becomes.

principles.name: Immediacy
principles.note: The closer a group is to an individual, the more likely the individual is to comply.

principles.name: Number
principles.note: Compliance generally increases with group size, with diminishing influence after about four or five people.

principles.name: norm of reciprocity
principles.note: People tend to return a favor when one has been granted to them.

methods.name: foot-in-the-door technique
methods.note: A small request is followed by a larger request.

methods.name: door-in-the-face
methods.note: A large request expected to be refused is followed by a more reasonable request.

methods.name: low-ball
methods.note: An initially attractive low price is increased at the last moment.

methods.name: ingratiation
methods.note: Gaining someone's approval so they are more likely to accept demands.

methods.name: self-presentation
methods.note: Presenting one's attributes in a manner appealing to the target.

theories.name: social impact theory
theories.note: Bibb Latané's theory that social impact is governed by strength, immediacy, and number.

frameworks.name: SIFT-3M Model
frameworks.note: David Straker's nine-stage model of mental functioning in compliance decisions.

concepts.name: confidence
concepts.note: The feeling of belief or trust that a person or thing is reliable.

concepts.name: self-confidence
concepts.note: Trust in oneself and a positive belief in one's ability to accomplish what one wishes.

concepts.name: self-esteem
concepts.note: An evaluation of one's worth.

concepts.name: self-efficacy
concepts.note: Albert Bandura's belief in one's ability to succeed in specific situations or accomplish a task.

concepts.name: self-actualization
concepts.note: The desire that follows the attainment of self-confidence in Maslow's account.

concepts.name: self-fulfilling prophecy
concepts.note: A process in which confidence or its absence contributes to the expected success or failure.

theories.name: A Theory of Human Motivation
theories.note: Abraham Maslow's theory placing self-confidence within esteem and describing its relation to self-actualization.

concepts.name: contingency
concepts.note: The feature of a statement making it neither necessary nor impossible.

concepts.name: necessity
concepts.note: A modal status in which a statement cannot be false in any possible world.

concepts.name: possibility
concepts.note: A status in which a statement is true in at least one possible world.

concepts.name: impossibility
concepts.note: A status in which no possible world can make a statement true.

concepts.name: possible world
concepts.note: A conceived world in which a statement may be true without contradicting another truth.

concepts.name: future contingency
concepts.note: The problem concerning the truth status of statements about future events.

theories.name: modal logic
theories.note: The study of the manner or mode in which statements are true.

theories.name: logical determinism
theories.note: The position at issue in Aristotle's treatment of future contingent statements.

concepts.name: cooperation
concepts.note: Working or acting together for collective benefit rather than selfish individual benefit.

concepts.name: emergence
concepts.note: A complex global property produced by components working together.

concepts.name: self-organization
concepts.note: The process considered to produce emergence in cooperating systems.

concepts.name: prisoner's dilemma
concepts.note: A model showing that group members may fail to cooperate despite mutual benefit.

theories.name: game theory
theories.note: The theoretical framework used to formalize the prisoner's dilemma.

frameworks.name: five mechanisms for the evolution of cooperation
frameworks.note: Kin selection, direct reciprocity, indirect reciprocity, spatial structure, and group selection.

concepts.name: coping
concepts.note: The application of conscious and unconscious cognitions used to manage unpleasant emotions, stress, and anxiety.

concepts.name: adaptive coping
concepts.note: Coping mechanisms that successfully improve the user's well-being.

concepts.name: maladaptive coping
concepts.note: Coping that manages an emotion at the expense of other mental or physical health.

concepts.name: proactive coping
concepts.note: Coping aimed at preparing for or preventing future stressors.

concepts.name: problem-focused coping
concepts.note: Coping directed at addressing the source of stress.

concepts.name: emotion-focused coping
concepts.note: Coping oriented toward managing emotions accompanying perceived stress.

methods.name: taking control
methods.note: A problem-focused approach identified by Folkman and Lazarus.

methods.name: information seeking
methods.note: A problem-focused approach involving gathering information about the stressor.

methods.name: evaluating pros and cons
methods.note: A problem-focused approach for assessing alternatives.

methods.name: mindfulness practices
methods.note: An emotion-focused coping strategy.

methods.name: systematic relaxation procedures
methods.note: An emotion-focused coping strategy for managing stress-related emotions.

theories.name: Health Theory of Coping
theories.note: A theory classifying coping strategies as healthy or unhealthy according to likely outcomes.

frameworks.name: four main types of coping
frameworks.note: Folkman and Lazarus's classification: problem-focused, emotion-focused, support-seeking, and meaning-making coping.

frameworks.name: healthy coping categories
frameworks.note: Self-soothing, relaxation/distraction, social support, and professional support.

frameworks.name: unhealthy coping categories
frameworks.note: Negative self-talk, harmful activities, social withdrawal, and suicidality.

concepts.name: counterdependency
concepts.note: Refusal of attachment, denial of personal need and dependency, and sometimes refusal of dialogue.

concepts.name: counterdependent personality
concepts.note: A personality described as addicted to activity, grandiose, strong-acting, and pushing others away.

concepts.name: negative transference
concepts.note: A form in which counterdependency can present in a clinical situation.

concepts.name: counterdependent transference
concepts.note: In George Kelly's personal construct theory, the therapist's transference of dependency onto the client.

theories.name: personal construct theory
theories.note: George Kelly's theory in which counterdependent transference has a distinct meaning.

theories.name: attachment theory
theories.note: The developmental context discussed in relation to attachment, dependency, and distancing.

concepts.name: Counterfactual thinking
concepts.note: The tendency to create possible alternatives to events that have already occurred.

concepts.name: Upward counterfactuals
concepts.note: Thoughts about how a situation could have been better.

concepts.name: Downward counterfactuals
concepts.note: Thoughts about how a situation could have been worse.

concepts.name: Additive counterfactuals
concepts.note: Imagining the addition of an event that did not occur.

concepts.name: Subtractive counterfactuals
concepts.note: Imagining the deletion of an action or event that occurred.

concepts.name: Self-focused counterfactuals
concepts.note: Counterfactuals focusing on actions performed by the self.

concepts.name: Other-focused counterfactuals
concepts.note: Counterfactuals focusing on actions performed by others.

principles.name: Contrast effect
principles.note: A judgment becomes more extreme through juxtaposition with an anchor or standard.

frameworks.name: Activation and content
frameworks.note: Counterfactual thinking has an activation portion and a content portion.

coined_terms.name: Signal anxiety
coined_terms.note: Anna Freud introduced the concept in 1936 as a signal in the ego of anticipated instinctual tension.

concepts.name: Object constancy
concepts.note: Knowing that good and bad can exist at the same time in the same person.

concepts.name: Defence mechanism
concepts.note: An unconscious psychological process protecting the self from anxiety-producing thoughts and feelings.

concepts.name: Mechanisms of adaptation
concepts.note: Defence and coping mechanisms working together to balance anxiety or guilt.

theories.name: Psychoanalytic theory
theories.note: A theory in which defence mechanisms protect the self from internal conflicts and external stressors.

frameworks.name: Vaillant's categorization
frameworks.note: George Eman Vaillant's four-level classification of pathological, immature, neurotic and mature defences.

frameworks.name: Defence Mechanism Rating Scale
frameworks.note: A scale dividing thirty defence processes into seven categories.

concepts.name: Dignity
concepts.note: The right to be valued and respected for one's own sake and treated ethically.

concepts.name: Human dignity
concepts.note: The worth of human beings and their entitlement to respect and ethical treatment.

concepts.name: Dignitas
concepts.note: A Latin concept variously translated as worthiness or prestige.

concepts.name: Humiliation
concepts.note: Acts that humiliate or diminish a person's or group's self-worth.

concepts.name: Instrumentalization or objectification
concepts.note: Treating a person as an instrument or means to achieve another goal.

concepts.name: Degradation
concepts.note: Acts that diminish the value of human beings.

concepts.name: Dehumanization
concepts.note: Acts that strip a person or group of human characteristics.

axioms.name: Ends in themselves
axioms.note: Kant's foundational idea that persons have ultimate moral worth and must not be treated merely as means.

principles.name: Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Article 1
principles.note: All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights.

concepts.name: Emotional self-regulation
concepts.note: The ability to respond to ongoing experience with socially tolerable and flexible emotional reactions.

concepts.name: Emotion dysregulation
concepts.note: Difficulty controlling emotional arousal's influence on thoughts, actions and interactions.

concepts.name: Situation selection
concepts.note: Choosing to avoid or approach a future emotional situation.

concepts.name: Situation modification
concepts.note: Changing a situation to alter its emotional impact.

concepts.name: Attentional deployment
concepts.note: Directing attention toward or away from an emotional situation.

concepts.name: Cognitive change
concepts.note: Changing appraisal of a situation to alter its emotional meaning.

concepts.name: Response modulation
concepts.note: Directly influencing experiential, behavioral or physiological response systems.

methods.name: Reappraisal
methods.note: Changing the meaning of an event to alter its emotional impact.

methods.name: Distraction
methods.note: Diverting attention away from an emotional stimulus toward other content.

methods.name: Expressive suppression
methods.note: Inhibiting emotional expressions.

frameworks.name: Process model of emotion regulation
frameworks.note: A model identifying five regulation families corresponding to points in emotion generation.

frameworks.name: Modal model of emotion
frameworks.note: A sequence of situation, attention, appraisal and response, with a feedback loop.

frameworks.name: Model of the Cognitive Control of Emotion (MCCE)
frameworks.note: A model tracing stimulus processing through attention, appraisal and response.

concepts.name: Empirical evidence
concepts.note: Evidence obtained through sense experience or experimental procedure.

concepts.name: A posteriori knowledge
concepts.note: Knowledge whose justification or falsification depends on experience or experiment.

concepts.name: A priori knowledge
concepts.note: Knowledge treated as innate or justified by rational intuition rather than empirical evidence.

concepts.name: Scientific evidence
concepts.note: Evidence arrived at by following scientific method within a scientific theory.

concepts.name: Observation
concepts.note: Passive sensing of phenomena without manipulation or intervention.

concepts.name: Experimentation
concepts.note: Active creation or manipulation of phenomena through intervention.

methods.name: Scientific method
methods.note: A process involving hypothesis formation, experimental design, peer review and reproduction of results.

methods.name: Semi-empirical methods
methods.note: Theoretical methods using basic axioms or postulated laws together with experimental results.

methods.name: Ab initio methods
methods.note: Purely deductive theoretical methods based on first principles.

theories.name: Empiricism
theories.note: The view that all knowledge or epistemic justification arises from experience.

theories.name: Rationalism
theories.note: The view that some knowledge is independent of experience and justified by reason.

concepts.name: Equity
concepts.note: A body of law developed in the English Court of Chancery to supplement inflexible common-law rules.

concepts.name: Epieikeia
concepts.note: Aristotle's concept of equity as a correction when universal law is unjust in a specific case.

concepts.name: Equitable interest
concepts.note: A legal interest arising from equitable title and protected by equitable remedies.

concepts.name: Equitable trust
concepts.note: A legal relationship in which property is managed by a trustee for a beneficiary.

concepts.name: Resulting trust
concepts.note: An implied trust working out the presumed intentions of the parties.

concepts.name: Constructive trust
concepts.note: A trust implied by law to work out justice regardless of the parties' intentions.

axioms.name: Ubi jus ibi remedium
axioms.note: The legal maxim that where there is a right, there must be a remedy.

principles.name: Good faith
principles.note: An equitable principle included among the doctrines developed by equity.

principles.name: Equity acts in personam rather than in rem
principles.note: The historical maxim that equity acts against persons rather than things.

frameworks.name: Maxims of equity
frameworks.note: A set of general legal maxims governing the operation of equity.

concepts.name: Evidentialism
concepts.note: The thesis that a person is justified in believing something if and only if they have supporting evidence.

concepts.name: Epistemic justification
concepts.note: Justification of a belief relative to the epistemic goal of having beliefs likely to be true.

concepts.name: Pragmatic or prudential justification
concepts.note: Justification of a belief for promoting some practical goal.

concepts.name: Properly basic beliefs
concepts.note: Beliefs justified without being based on other beliefs.

axioms.name: EJ
axioms.note: A doxastic attitude D toward proposition p is epistemically justified for S at t iff having D toward p fits the evidence.

theories.name: Foundationalism
theories.note: The view that some beliefs are justified without being based on other beliefs.

theories.name: Coherentism
theories.note: The view that beliefs are mutually supported in a coherent network, potentially through circular support.

theories.name: Skepticism
theories.note: The view that there cannot be any justified beliefs.

theories.name: Infinitism
theories.note: The view that evidential chains may continue through infinite chains of reasons.

theories.name: Reliabilism
theories.note: The theory that a belief is justified when caused by a reliable belief-forming process.

theories.name: Causal theory
theories.note: The theory that knowledge requires an appropriate causal connection between fact and belief.

theories.name: Truth tracking theory
theories.note: Robert Nozick's theory that knowledge requires a belief to track the truth value of a proposition.

concepts.name: Exercise
concepts.note: Physical activity that enhances or maintains fitness and overall health.

concepts.name: Aerobic exercise
concepts.note: Activity using large muscle groups and more oxygen than at rest.

concepts.name: Anaerobic exercise
concepts.note: Exercise including strength and resistance training that improves short-term muscle strength.

concepts.name: Flexibility exercises
concepts.note: Exercises that stretch and lengthen muscles to improve range of motion.

concepts.name: Dynamic exercise
concepts.note: Exercise such as steady running that tends to lower diastolic blood pressure during exercise.

concepts.name: Static exercise
concepts.note: Exercise such as weight-lifting that can transiently raise systolic pressure.

methods.name: 4-Rs framework
methods.note: Recovery framework of Rehydration, Refuel, Repair and Rest.

concepts.name: Exposure therapy
concepts.note: A behavior-therapy technique exposing a patient to an anxiety source or its context without intending danger.

concepts.name: Exposure and response prevention (ERP or ExRP)
concepts.note: Exposure in which refraining from the escape response is maintained at all times.

concepts.name: Exposure hierarchy
concepts.note: A series of progressively stronger fear-inducing stimuli or challenges.

concepts.name: Pavlovian extinction
concepts.note: The respondent-conditioning principle on which exposure therapy is based.

principles.name: Respondent conditioning
principles.note: The conditioning principle underlying exposure therapy.

principles.name: Reciprocal inhibition
principles.note: The idea that anxiety and relaxation cannot coexist simultaneously.

methods.name: In vivo
methods.note: Exposure to actual fear-inducing situations.

methods.name: Virtual reality
methods.note: Technology used to simulate in-vivo exposure.

methods.name: Imaginal
methods.note: Having patients imagine a feared situation.

methods.name: Written exposure therapy
methods.note: Having patients write an account of a traumatic event.

methods.name: Interoceptive
methods.note: Having patients confront feared bodily symptoms.

methods.name: Flooding therapy
methods.note: Exposure beginning with the most feared item in a fear hierarchy.

methods.name: Self Distancing
methods.note: A cognitive strategy of referring to oneself in the third person to gain perspective.

frameworks.name: Method of Factors
frameworks.note: A dynamic hierarchy approach identifying stimulus features that control fear intensity during exposure.

concepts.name: fact
concepts.note: A true datum about a circumstance or occurrence in the real world.

concepts.name: scientific fact
concepts.note: An objective, verifiable observation from repeatable observation or measurement.

concepts.name: empirical evidence
concepts.note: Observation or measurement by experimentation or other means.

concepts.name: justified true belief
concepts.note: An Enlightenment-era definition of knowledge encompassing facts.

methods.name: scientific method
methods.note: Observation, measurement and experimentation used to investigate facts.

methods.name: peer review
methods.note: Institutional review intended to promote factual accuracy.

concepts.name: feedback
concepts.note: Routing outputs back as inputs in a causal circuit or loop.

concepts.name: positive feedback
concepts.note: Feedback in phase with the input, or feedback that widens a gap.

concepts.name: negative feedback
concepts.note: Feedback 180 degrees out of phase with the input, or feedback that narrows a gap.

concepts.name: feedback loop
concepts.note: A causal chain in which a system feeds back into itself.

methods.name: state space
methods.note: A control-theory method for feedback.

methods.name: full state feedback
methods.note: A feedback method used in control theory.

theories.name: control theory
theories.note: The field in which feedback is extensively used to control systems.

concepts.name: goal commitment
concepts.note: Commitment to achieving a specific goal.

concepts.name: goal acceptance
concepts.note: Willingness to pursue a specific goal.

concepts.name: self-efficacy
concepts.note: Belief that one is able to achieve one's goals.

concepts.name: superordinate goals
concepts.note: Goals at a higher level of abstraction in a goal hierarchy.

principles.name: principle of diminishing returns

principles.name: principle of goal specificity

principles.name: principle of goal difficulty
principles.note: Higher goals produce higher performance when commitment exists.

methods.name: goal setting
methods.note: Developing an action plan to motivate and guide a person or group toward a goal.

methods.name: quantification
methods.note: Making a goal measurable.

methods.name: enumeration
methods.note: Defining tasks required to achieve a goal.

methods.name: error management training

theories.name: goal-setting theory
theories.note: Locke and colleagues' theory relating difficult specific goals to performance.

theories.name: temporal motivation theory
theories.note: A theory explaining goal-setting effects through goal difficulty and proximity.

frameworks.name: SMART criteria

frameworks.name: objectives and key results model
frameworks.note: A business model using measurable, time-bound key results.

coined_terms.name: Golden Rule

concepts.name: ethics of reciprocity
concepts.note: Reciprocating to others how one would like to be treated.

concepts.name: Silver Rule
concepts.note: The negative form: do not treat others as one would not want to be treated.

concepts.name: habit
concepts.note: A routine of behavior repeated regularly and tending to occur subconsciously.

concepts.name: automaticity

frameworks.name: five levels of regulation of behaviour

frameworks.name: four main components to habit formation
frameworks.note: Context cue, craving, behavioral repetition and reward.

concepts.name: hexis
concepts.note: A relatively stable arrangement or disposition such as health, knowledge or character.

concepts.name: disposition
concepts.note: An arrangement of what has parts in space, potentiality or form.

concepts.name: diathesis
concepts.note: A passive, shallow disposition easier to remove or change than a hexis.

concepts.name: habitus
concepts.note: The Latin term traditionally used to translate hexis.

coined_terms.name: illusion of control
coined_terms.note: Named by American psychologist Ellen Langer.

concepts.name: introspection illusion
concepts.note: Lack of direct introspective insight into whether one controls events.

concepts.name: skill cues

frameworks.name: positive illusions

frameworks.name: three converging lines of evidence

concepts.name: impartiality
concepts.note: A choice property in which a specified consideration has no influence.

concepts.name: impartial point of view
concepts.note: The standpoint from which moral questions are judged.

concepts.name: impartial spectator

concepts.name: partialist–impartialist debate
concepts.note: Disagreement over impartiality and special concern for close relations.

axioms.name: the good of any one individual is of no more importance
axioms.note: Sidgwick's claim that one person's good is no more important than another's from the Universe's viewpoint.

principles.name: equal respect for every person as an end in themselves
principles.note: The Kantian requirement expressing impartiality.

principles.name: first-order impartiality
principles.note: Impartiality governing individual choices.

principles.name: second-order impartiality
principles.note: Impartiality governing the choice of rules.

theories.name: ideal observer theory
theories.note: Moral judgments are those an ideal, informed and disinterested observer would make.

theories.name: consequentialist impartiality
theories.note: Counting everyone's well-being equally when assessing outcomes.

theories.name: Kantian ethics
theories.note: Requiring universalizable maxims and equal respect for persons.

theories.name: contractualism
theories.note: Building impartiality into hypothetical agreement conditions.

frameworks.name: original position
frameworks.note: Rawls's standpoint for choosing justice principles behind a veil of ignorance.

frameworks.name: veil of ignorance
frameworks.note: A device hiding one's social position so principles cannot favor oneself.

concepts.name: inference
concepts.note: A conclusion reached from evidence and reasoning, or that process.

concepts.name: deduction
concepts.note: Inference deriving logical conclusions from premises.

concepts.name: induction
concepts.note: Inference from particular evidence to a universal conclusion.

concepts.name: abduction
concepts.note: Inference seeking the best explanation based on likelihood.

concepts.name: fallacy

principles.name: Bayes' theorem
principles.note: The central rule of Bayesian inference.

methods.name: statistical inference
methods.note: Using mathematics to draw conclusions amid uncertainty.

methods.name: Bayesian inference
methods.note: Using probability rules to identify the best explanation.

frameworks.name: Bayesian framework
frameworks.note: A probability framework treating probabilities as degrees of belief.

frameworks.name: inference system
frameworks.note: A system that automatically extends a knowledge base through valid inferences.

concepts.name: Inhibitory control

concepts.name: Response inhibition
concepts.note: Another name for inhibitory control.

concepts.name: Self-control
concepts.note: An important aspect of inhibitory control.

concepts.name: Prepotent responses
concepts.note: Natural, habitual, or dominant behavioral responses to stimuli.

methods.name: Stroop task
methods.note: A neuropsychological test used to measure inhibitory control.

methods.name: Go/no-go task

concepts.name: Integrity
concepts.note: The quality of being honest and consistently adhering to strong moral and ethical principles and values.

concepts.name: Internal consistency
concepts.note: The consistency of a person's values and actions, treated as a virtue.

concepts.name: Worldview
concepts.note: A comprehensive corpus of beliefs associated with the wholeness implied by integrity.

concepts.name: Moral responsibility
concepts.note: Accountability for flexibly adjusting values to maintain consistency when challenged.

axioms.name: Logical axioms or postulates
axioms.note: Foundational assumptions to which principles should uniformly adhere.

principles.name: Moral and ethical principles
principles.note: Strong principles and values to which integrity involves consistent and uncompromising adherence.

theories.name: Positive Model of Integrity
theories.note: Michael Jensen and Werner Erhard's model of integrity as being whole, complete, sound, and unimpaired.

frameworks.name: Internally consistent framework of principles
frameworks.note: The framework on which a person's actions are based when the person possesses ethical integrity.

frameworks.name: Multifaceted perspective of integrity
frameworks.note: Muel Kaptein's view that integrity includes compliance with rules and social expectations, morality and ethics, and actions and attitude.

concepts.name: Interpersonal interdependence
concepts.note: The process by which interacting people influence one another's experiences.

concepts.name: Actor Control
concepts.note: The impact of an individual's behavior on that individual's outcomes.

concepts.name: Partner Control
concepts.note: The impact of one individual's behavior on the outcomes of the other individual in the interaction.

concepts.name: Joint Control
concepts.note: The joint impact of each individual's behavior on each individual's outcome.

concepts.name: Mutuality of dependence
concepts.note: A dimension concerning the level and equality of dependence between interaction partners.

principles.name: The Principle of Structure
principles.note: Interpersonal situations have definable patterns of interdependence that shape interaction.

principles.name: The Principle of Transformation
principles.note: People may transform a situation according to motivations, values, and broader relationship goals.

principles.name: The Principle of Interaction
principles.note: Relationship outcomes are determined by the mutual influence of both parties' actions.

principles.name: The Principle of Adaptation
principles.note: Individuals develop behavioral patterns over time in response to recurring interdependent situations.

theories.name: Interdependence theory
theories.note: A social exchange theory analyzing how interpersonal outcomes depend on one's own and others' actions.

frameworks.name: SABI model
frameworks.note: A model expressing interactions as a function of Person A, Person B, and the situation: I = ƒ[A, B, S].

coined_terms.name: Metamotivation
coined_terms.note: Abraham Maslow coined the term in his later writings for motivation beyond basic needs; it concerns striving for constant betterment.

concepts.name: Physiological needs
concepts.note: The most prepotent basic needs in Maslow's hierarchy.

concepts.name: Safety needs
concepts.note: Basic needs that emerge after physiological needs are fairly fulfilled.

concepts.name: Love needs
concepts.note: The higher need involving giving and receiving love.

concepts.name: Esteem needs
concepts.note: The need that follows love in the original hierarchy.

concepts.name: Self-actualization needs
concepts.note: The highest level in the original five-level hierarchy.

concepts.name: Meta-needs
concepts.note: A sixth level added by Maslow in later writings.

concepts.name: Deficiency needs
concepts.note: Needs whose deprivation motivates people to fulfill what they are denied.

theories.name: Maslow's theory
theories.note: The theory that humans are compelled to satisfy physiological needs before pursuing higher-level needs.

frameworks.name: Maslow's hierarchy of needs
frameworks.note: A hierarchy of five sets of basic needs ordered by prepotency: physiological, safety, love, esteem, and self-actualization.

concepts.name: Meaning
concepts.note: How people make sense of and give meaning to their existence.

concepts.name: Existence precedes essence
concepts.note: The view that humans exist first and must achieve or create meaning rather than receive it as a pre-given essence.

concepts.name: Subjectivism
concepts.note: An approach holding that meaning is grounded in what people find meaningful or want from life.

concepts.name: Will to meaning
concepts.note: The motivation to find meaning in life.

principles.name: Life has meaning under all circumstances
principles.note: A basic principle of logotherapy, including under the most miserable circumstances.

principles.name: Our main motivation for living is our will to find meaning in life
principles.note: A basic principle of logotherapy.

principles.name: We have inalienable freedom to find meaning
principles.note: A basic principle of logotherapy.

methods.name: Logotherapy
methods.note: A psychological analysis and therapeutic approach focused on a will to meaning.

theories.name: Subjectivist theories
theories.note: Theories holding that meaning is grounded in what people find meaningful or want out of life.

frameworks.name: Three ways of finding meaning
frameworks.note: Meaning can be found by creating a work or doing a deed, experiencing something or encountering someone, or adopting an attitude toward unavoidable suffering.

concepts.name: Meaningful life
concepts.note: A construct concerning the purpose, significance, fulfillment, and satisfaction of life.

concepts.name: Creative values
concepts.note: Values reached through creating or producing something.

concepts.name: Experiential values
concepts.note: Values actualized through experiencing something with the senses.

concepts.name: Attitudinal values
concepts.note: Values found by adopting a new attitude when new experiences or creation are unavailable.

concepts.name: Sense of purpose
concepts.note: One of Baumeister's four needs that constitute meaningfulness.

concepts.name: Efficacy
concepts.note: One of Baumeister's four needs that constitute meaningfulness.

concepts.name: Value
concepts.note: One of Baumeister's four needs that constitute meaningfulness.

concepts.name: Positive self-worth
concepts.note: One of Baumeister's four needs that constitute meaningfulness.

theories.name: Hope theory
theories.note: A theory that operationalizes meaningfulness as involving self-control leading to higher self-esteem.

theories.name: Narrative psychology
theories.note: The view that people construct life stories to understand events and impose meaning on life.

theories.name: Terror management theory
theories.note: A theory discussed in relation to meaningfulness.

frameworks.name: Three classes of values
frameworks.note: Logotherapy's classification of values as creative, experiential, and attitudinal.

concepts.name: Mercy
concepts.note: Benevolence, forgiveness, and kindness in ethical, religious, social, and legal contexts.

concepts.name: Clemency
concepts.note: The term often used for mercy in a judicial context.

concepts.name: Grace
concepts.note: God's favor or divine assistance, distinguished from mercy as what one receives when one does not get what one deserves.

concepts.name: Works of Mercy
concepts.note: Acts such as giving alms and caring for the sick emphasized as components of religious belief.

concepts.name: Mindfulness
concepts.note: The cognitive skill or state of intentionally maintaining moment-by-moment, nonjudgmental awareness of experience.

concepts.name: Formal mindfulness
concepts.note: Meditation that sustains attention on the body, breath, sensations, or whatever arises.

concepts.name: Informal mindfulness
concepts.note: The application of mindful attention in everyday life.

methods.name: Meditation
methods.note: The usual means by which mindfulness is developed.

methods.name: Breathing meditation
methods.note: A practice of attending to natural breathing while noticing and accepting mind-wandering.

methods.name: Body-scan meditation
methods.note: A practice directing attention to different body areas and noting present sensations.

methods.name: Mindful tasting of a raisin
methods.note: A Kabat-Zinn exercise in which a raisin is tasted and eaten mindfully.

methods.name: Nonmeditation-based exercises
methods.note: Exercises used in dialectical behavior therapy and acceptance and commitment therapy to develop mindfulness.

concepts.name: Mindset
concepts.note: An established set of attitudes concerning culture, values, philosophy, frame of reference, outlook, or disposition.

concepts.name: Theory of mind
concepts.note: A person's theory about another person, relating mindset research to theory-of-mind research.

concepts.name: Growth mindset
concepts.note: The belief that intelligence and abilities can be developed through learning and effort.

concepts.name: Deliberative mindset
concepts.note: A mindset in which a person considers various actions without yet deciding what to do.

concepts.name: Promotion mindset
concepts.note: A motivational orientation focused on achievement and accomplishment.

concepts.name: Prevention mindset
concepts.note: A motivational orientation focused on avoiding negative outcomes and fulfilling duties.

theories.name: Mindscape theory
theories.note: A theory that measures individuals on characteristics and places them into one of four personality categories.

frameworks.name: Three bipolar dimensions of culture
frameworks.note: Sagiv and Schwartz's dimensions: cognitive (embedded or autonomous), figurative (mastery or harmony), and operative (hierarchical or egalitarian).

frameworks.name: Myers–Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI)
frameworks.note: An instrument measuring psychological functions and social attitudes to generate personality types.

coined_terms.name: character

concepts.name: Moral character

concepts.name: Moral virtue
concepts.note: An excellence of character: qualities that make a person ethically admirable.

concepts.name: Moral vice

concepts.name: Continence

concepts.name: Incontinence

concepts.name: Applied ethics

axioms.name: Excellence of character

principles.name: Virtue ethics
principles.note: An approach centered on virtue and the qualities of morally admirable character.

principles.name: Fruit of the Holy Spirit
principles.note: Christian character expressed through love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control.

concepts.name: Motivation

concepts.name: Amotivation
concepts.note: A lack of interest in an activity or resistance to it.

concepts.name: Intrinsic motivation

concepts.name: Extrinsic motivation
concepts.note: Motivation arising from external factors such as rewards or punishment.

concepts.name: Conscious motivation
concepts.note: Motives of which the person is aware.

concepts.name: Unconscious motivation
concepts.note: Motives of which the person is not aware.

concepts.name: Rational motivation
concepts.note: Motivation based on a good reason for acting.

concepts.name: Altruistic motivation
concepts.note: Motivation involving concern for others without personal gain.

theories.name: Self-determination theory

frameworks.name: Content theories

frameworks.name: Process theories

frameworks.name: Goal-setting and goal-striving

concepts.name: Natural rights

concepts.name: Positive law
concepts.note: Enacted law associated with legal rights.

concepts.note: Rights arising from a social contract rather than natural or positive law.

concepts.note: Rights traditionally understood as limits on what government may do.

concepts.name: Positive rights

theories.name: Natural rights theory

theories.name: Social contract
theories.note: An agreement among members of a country to live within a shared system of laws.

concepts.name: Nonattachment

concepts.name: Detachment

concepts.name: Apatheia
concepts.note: Christian and Stoic detachment from worldly objects, passions, and concerns.

concepts.name: Upādāna
concepts.note: The opposite of detachment, translated as attachment.

concepts.name: Nekkhamma
concepts.note: Buddhist renunciation, including giving up the world and freedom from lust and craving.

concepts.name: Wú niàn
concepts.note: Chinese term meaning “no thought,” or being unstained by thought.

concepts.name: Vairagya

concepts.name: Eudaimonia

principles.note: One of Jainism’s five great vows observed by Jain monks.

principles.name: Equanimity
principles.note: The Stoic quality of responding rationally without emotional or egotistical reaction to uncontrollable events.

methods.name: Ignatian spirituality

concepts.name: Occupational burnout

concepts.name: Emotional exhaustion

concepts.name: Reduced personal accomplishment

concepts.name: Cynicism

methods.name: Cognitive restructuring
methods.note: An intervention suggested for burnout symptoms.

methods.name: Graded activity
methods.note: An intervention suggested for workers with burnout symptoms.

methods.name: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT)
methods.note: A treatment reported as useful especially for exhaustion and poor sleep.

methods.name: Mindfulness therapy

methods.name: Stress management

methods.name: Time management

methods.name: Occupational therapy

frameworks.name: Secondary prevention

frameworks.name: Tertiary prevention

concepts.name: Overprecision

concepts.name: Illusion of control
concepts.note: The tendency to behave as if one has control when one has none.

concepts.name: Planning fallacy
concepts.note: Overestimating work rate or underestimating the time needed to complete tasks.

concepts.name: Comparative optimism
concepts.note: Believing good events are more likely and bad events less likely to happen to oneself than to others.

concepts.name: Lake Wobegon effect
concepts.note: The claim or tendency that nearly everyone considers their performance above average.

methods.name: Confidence intervals

concepts.name: Persistence

concepts.name: Reward dependence (RD)

concepts.name: Cooperativeness (CO)

concepts.name: Self-transcendence (SF)

concepts.name: Self-directedness (SD)

frameworks.name: TCI-R

concepts.name: Personal boundaries

concepts.name: Containment
concepts.note: The function of boundaries concerning outgoing interactions.

concepts.name: Physical boundaries

concepts.name: Mental boundaries
concepts.note: Boundaries involving thoughts and opinions.

concepts.note: Boundaries involving feelings and emotional intimacy.

frameworks.note: Boundaries agreed upon, tacitly or explicitly, by everyone in a relationship group.

concepts.name: Adolescent egocentrism
concepts.note: A self-centered mode of thought associated with the formal operational stage.

concepts.name: Uniqueness
