concepts.name: Invulnerability
concepts.note: The belief that one cannot be harmed or affected as others can.

concepts.name: Omnipotence
concepts.note: The belief that one has great authority or power and can do what most others cannot.

concepts.name: Self-compassion
concepts.note: Relating to oneself amid inadequacy or difficulty with warmth, connection, and concern.

methods.name: Personal Fable Scale
methods.note: An 18-item scale assessing speciality, invulnerability, and risk-taking dimensions.

theories.name: Piagetian theory
theories.note: The theory placing the personal fable and imaginary audience in the formal operational stage.

theories.name: Theory of mind
theories.note: The developing ability to understand or speculate about what others are thinking.

frameworks.name: Three subtypes of the personal fable
frameworks.note: A scheme distinguishing omnipotence, invulnerability, and uniqueness.

frameworks.name: Self-compassion’s three components
frameworks.note: Self-kindness, common humanity, and mindfulness.

concepts.name: premise
concepts.note: A proposition or assumption offered to support a conclusion and serve as a starting point for reasoning.

concepts.name: explicit premise
concepts.note: A premise overtly stated in the text.

concepts.name: implicit premise
concepts.note: A premise tacitly assumed without appearing in the text.

concepts.name: independent premise
concepts.note: A premise that presents a distinct reason supporting the conclusion.

concepts.name: dependent premise
concepts.note: A premise that works only in combination with other premises.

methods.name: standard form
methods.note: A way of writing each premise on a separate line.

theories.name: argumentation theory
theories.note: The field concerned with arguments, their premises, conclusions, and support relations.

concepts.name: presupposition
concepts.note: An implicit assumption about the world or background belief taken for granted by an utterance.

concepts.name: presupposition trigger
concepts.note: A lexical item or linguistic construction responsible for triggering a presupposition.

concepts.name: common ground
concepts.note: The shared knowledge of interlocutors that normally contains a sentence’s presupposition.

concepts.name: presupposition accommodation
concepts.note: The addressee’s process of assuming a presupposition is true despite no explicit information.

concepts.name: entailment
concepts.note: A relation in which an expression guarantees another proposition, unlike presupposition under negation.

concepts.name: implicature
concepts.note: An inferred meaning distinguished from presupposition and entailment.

concepts.name: prioritization
concepts.note: The activity of arranging items or activities in order of urgency.

concepts.name: priority setting
concepts.note: Establishing the importance or urgency of actions, especially when resources are limited.

methods.name: risk priority number assessment
methods.note: A way to establish priorities that may be difficult to determine in a health-care setting.

concepts.name: neuromuscular adaptation
concepts.note: An early adaptation to strength training that increases lifting strength.

concepts.name: overtraining
concepts.note: A decline in training performance often accompanied by greater illness or injury risk and reduced desire to exercise.

principles.name: progressive overload
principles.note: Stress must increase as the body adapts in order to sustain further adaptation.

methods.name: resistance training
methods.note: Training that places exercise musculature under greater-than-normal demand.

methods.name: periodization
methods.note: Scheduling recovery and variety while applying different load-progression strategies over a long-term program.

concepts.name: psychological distance
concepts.note: The degree to which people feel removed from a phenomenon, including separation from persons, events, knowledge, or time.

concepts.name: temporal distance
concepts.note: Distance involving separation in time.

concepts.name: spatial distance
concepts.note: Distance involving physical or geographic separation.

concepts.name: social distance
concepts.note: Distance involving separation between people or social entities.

concepts.name: hypothetical distance
concepts.note: Distance involving how possible or certain an event is.

concepts.name: informational distance
concepts.note: Distance involving separation in knowledge or information.

theories.name: Construal Level Theory
theories.note: The theory in which psychological distance shapes the relationship between an event and a person and affects perceived importance.

frameworks.name: four categories of distance
frameworks.note: A scheme comprising temporal, spatial, social, hypothetical, and informational distance as described in the article.

concepts.name: psychological resilience
concepts.note: The ability to cope mentally and emotionally with a crisis or return quickly to pre-crisis status.

concepts.name: mental resilience
concepts.note: Another term for the ability to adapt during or after psychological adversity.

concepts.name: positive adaptation
concepts.note: A healthy adaptation following a stressful or adverse situation.

concepts.name: hardiness
concepts.note: An internal characteristic identified as influencing resilience.

concepts.name: psychological recovery
concepts.note: Returning to a prior mental state, contrasted with resisting adverse conditions.

frameworks.name: adversity and positive adaptation
frameworks.note: The two concepts around which most definitions of psychological resilience center.

concepts.name: rational choice model
concepts.note: A model using decision theory as guidelines for understanding economic and social behavior.

concepts.name: rational actor
concepts.note: An actor whose behavior is analyzed by balancing the same costs and benefits.

concepts.name: instrumental rationality
concepts.note: A view in which the path to a goal may or may not be included as a decision factor.

concepts.name: preference
concepts.note: An individual’s ordering of available choices used to decide on an action.

axioms.name: completeness
axioms.note: The assumption that an individual’s preferences can meaningfully compare the available alternatives.

axioms.name: transitivity
axioms.note: The assumption that preference orderings are logically consistent across alternatives.

principles.name: rational choice theory
principles.note: Behavior is rational when it is the logical outcome of stated preferences.

methods.name: cost–benefit analysis
methods.note: Balancing the costs and benefits of alternatives to understand or predict action.

theories.name: decision theory
theories.note: The theory used as a set of guidelines for understanding choice and behavior.

coined_terms.name: schema
coined_terms.note: Jean Piaget introduced the term in 1923 for a pattern or structure used in understanding experience.

coined_terms.name: schema theory
coined_terms.note: Richard C. Anderson expanded the schema idea into schema theory by 1977.

concepts.name: mental model
concepts.note: A mental representation or conceptual model of some aspect of the world.

concepts.name: social schema
concepts.note: A schema organizing knowledge about social people or situations.

concepts.name: stereotype
concepts.note: A schema involving generalized expectations about a category of people.

concepts.name: script
concepts.note: A schema representing an expected sequence of events or actions.

concepts.name: worldview
concepts.note: An organized way of understanding the world.

concepts.name: heuristic
concepts.note: A cognitive shortcut used to organize or interpret information.

concepts.name: archetype
concepts.note: A recurring or prototypical pattern included among examples of schemata.

methods.name: schematic processing
methods.note: Using schemata to encode and retrieve memories and organize new perceptions.

methods.name: schema therapy
methods.note: A psychotherapy developed by Jeffrey Young for treating personality disorders.

concepts.name: self-compassion
concepts.note: Extending compassion toward oneself during perceived inadequacy, failure, or suffering.

concepts.name: self-kindness
concepts.note: Being warm toward oneself during pain and shortcomings rather than using self-criticism.

concepts.name: common humanity
concepts.note: Recognizing that suffering and failure are part of shared human experience.

concepts.name: mindfulness
concepts.note: Observing negative thoughts and emotions openly and without suppression, exaggeration, or over-identification.

frameworks.name: three main elements of self-compassion
frameworks.note: Kristin Neff’s framework comprising self-kindness, common humanity, and mindfulness.

coined_terms.name: self-concept
coined_terms.note: Also called self-construction, self-identity, self-perspective, or self-structure; a collection of beliefs about oneself.

concepts.name: self-image
concepts.note: The view one has of oneself.

concepts.name: self-esteem
concepts.note: How much value one places on oneself.

concepts.name: ideal self
concepts.note: What one wishes one were really like.

concepts.name: social identity
concepts.note: The part of the self determined by membership in social groups.

concepts.name: possible selves
concepts.note: Ideas of what one might become, would like to become, or fears becoming.

concepts.name: self-schema
concepts.note: A self-assessment or belief about oneself that contributes to the overall self-concept.

methods.name: spontaneous self-report
methods.note: A method for measuring changes in self-concept by prompting a person with a question such as “Who are you?”

frameworks.name: Carl Rogers's three components of self-concept
frameworks.note: Self-image, self-esteem or self-worth, and ideal self.

coined_terms.name: introjective depression
coined_terms.note: Sidney Blatt theorized this term for a type of depression associated with self-criticism and achievement concerns.

concepts.name: self-criticism
concepts.note: How an individual evaluates oneself; it is typically discussed as a negative personality trait involving disrupted self-identity.

concepts.name: autonomy
concepts.note: The extent to which a person relies on preserving and increasing independence, mobility, and personal rights.

concepts.name: social dependency
concepts.note: A personality dimension relevant to depression in Aaron Beck’s account.

theories.name: Blatt's theory of introjective depression
theories.note: People who are highly self-critical and focused on achievement concerns are more likely to develop introjective depression.

frameworks.name: Blatt's two personality dimensions
frameworks.note: Two dimensions used to characterize personality in relation to depression.

frameworks.name: Beck's dimensions of personality
frameworks.note: Social dependency and autonomy as dimensions relevant to depression.

coined_terms.name: self-efficacy
coined_terms.note: Albert Bandura originally proposed the concept in 1977.

concepts.name: strong sense of self-efficacy
concepts.note: A belief that challenges can be mastered, supporting accomplishment and personal well-being.

concepts.name: observational learning
concepts.note: Learning through observing the actions of others.

concepts.name: social experience
concepts.note: External experience contributing to the development of self-efficacy and personality.

theories.name: self-efficacy theory
theories.note: Bandura’s account that beliefs about one’s ability to succeed influence goals, effort, persistence, feelings, and behavior.

theories.name: social cognitive theory
theories.note: A theory emphasizing observational learning and social experience in personality development.

concepts.name: self-esteem
concepts.note: Confidence in one’s own worth, abilities, or morals, including beliefs about oneself and related emotional states.

concepts.name: self-worth
concepts.note: A synonym or near-synonym of self-esteem.

concepts.name: self-regard
concepts.note: A synonym or near-synonym of self-esteem.

concepts.name: self-respect
concepts.note: A synonym or near-synonym of self-esteem.

concepts.name: self-integrity
concepts.note: A synonym or near-synonym of self-esteem.

concepts.name: trait self-esteem
concepts.note: Self-esteem regarded as an enduring personality characteristic.

concepts.name: state self-esteem
concepts.note: Normal, short-term variation in self-esteem.

methods.name: Rosenberg self-esteem scale (RSES)
methods.note: A widely used 10-item scale requiring agreement ratings on statements about oneself.

methods.name: Coopersmith Inventory
methods.note: A 50-question measure asking whether subjects rate someone as similar or dissimilar to themselves.

concepts.name: self-regulation
concepts.note: A system of conscious personal management that guides thoughts, behaviors, and feelings toward goals.

concepts.name: standards
concepts.note: Desirable behavior used as one component of self-regulation.

concepts.name: motivation
concepts.note: The drive to meet standards.

concepts.name: monitoring
concepts.note: Observation of situations and thoughts that precede breaking standards.

concepts.name: willpower
concepts.note: The internal capacity involved in self-regulation.

methods.name: goal clarification
methods.note: A structured intervention process for specifying goals.

methods.name: progress monitoring
methods.note: Tracking progress toward a goal.

methods.name: feedback loops
methods.note: Feedback-based processes used to strengthen emotional regulation and adaptive coping.

theories.name: self-regulation theory (SRT)
theories.note: A theory describing the process of guiding one’s thoughts, behaviors, and feelings to reach goals.

frameworks.name: self-regulation as a knowledge structure, strength, or skill
frameworks.note: Three models developed to explain the cognitive accessibility of self-regulation.

frameworks.name: Baumeister's four components of self-regulation
frameworks.note: Standards, motivation, monitoring, and willpower.

coined_terms.name: simulation heuristic
coined_terms.note: Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky first theorized it as a specialized adaptation of the availability heuristic.

concepts.name: counterfactual thinking
concepts.note: Thinking involving mentally undoing events and simulating alternatives.

concepts.name: regret
concepts.note: An emotion experienced more strongly for outcomes that are easier to imagine undoing.

methods.name: mental simulation
methods.note: Mentally undoing events and running simulations with altered input values.

theories.name: the theory underlying the simulation heuristic
theories.note: The account that judgments are biased toward information that is easily imagined or mentally simulated.

concepts.name: sleep
concepts.note: A state of reduced mental and physical activity with altered consciousness and inhibited sensory activity.

concepts.name: rapid eye movement sleep (REM)
concepts.note: A sleep mode associated with fast desynchronized brain waves, eye movements, loss of muscle tone, and dreams.

concepts.name: non-rapid eye movement sleep (non-REM or NREM)
concepts.note: The sleep type that occurs first and includes a transition to slow-wave or deep sleep.

concepts.name: slow-wave sleep
concepts.note: Deep sleep during which body temperature and heart rate fall and the brain uses less energy.

concepts.name: circadian clock
concepts.note: The internal clock that promotes sleep daily at night.

concepts.name: dreams
concepts.note: A succession of images, ideas, emotions, and sensations that usually occurs involuntarily during sleep.

methods.name: electroencephalography (EEG)
methods.note: Measurement of brain-wave activity during sleep.

methods.name: electrooculography (EOG)
methods.note: Measurement of eye movements during sleep.

methods.name: electromyography (EMG)
methods.note: Measurement of skeletal-muscle activity during sleep.

methods.name: polysomnography
methods.note: Simultaneous collection of EEG, EOG, and EMG measurements, often in a sleep laboratory.

methods.name: actigraphy
methods.note: Measurement of motor movements used by sleep researchers.

frameworks.name: American Academy of Sleep Medicine three-stage NREM classification
frameworks.note: NREM sleep is divided into N1, N2, and N3, with N3 also called delta or slow-wave sleep.

frameworks.name: sleep cycle
frameworks.note: The repeating alternation of NREM and REM sleep, normally proceeding N1 → N2 → N3 → N2 → REM.

coined_terms.name: golden circle
coined_terms.note: Simon Sinek’s name for the triad of Why, How, and What, represented as concentric circles.

concepts.name: Why
concepts.note: People’s motives or purposes, which Sinek says should come first in communication.

concepts.name: How
concepts.note: People’s processes or methods in the golden circle.

concepts.name: What
concepts.note: Results or outcomes in the golden circle.

concepts.name: inspiration
concepts.note: A way to influence behavior that Sinek argues is more powerful and sustainable than manipulation.

concepts.name: manipulation
concepts.note: One of the two main ways to influence human behavior discussed in the book.

principles.name: Start with Why
principles.note: The principle that communication should begin with purpose, then explain how and what.

frameworks.name: the golden circle
frameworks.note: A three-part concentric model with Why at the center, surrounded by How and then What.

coined_terms.name: stimulus
coined_terms.note: The term was coined in psychophysics in the second half of the 19th century in defining the scientific study of the relation between stimulus and sensation.

concepts.name: distal stimulus
concepts.note: The external, perceived object.

concepts.name: proximal stimulus
concepts.note: The stimulation of sensory organs.

concepts.name: unconditioned stimulus (US)
concepts.note: A stimulus that unconditionally triggers an unconditioned response.

concepts.name: conditioned stimulus (CS)
concepts.note: An originally irrelevant stimulus that triggers a conditioned response after conditioning.

concepts.name: eliciting stimulus
concepts.note: A stimulus that precedes a behavior and causes a response.

concepts.name: discriminative stimulus
concepts.note: A stimulus that increases the probability of a response without necessarily eliciting it.

concepts.name: reinforcing stimulus
concepts.note: A stimulus delivered after a response to reinforce the behavior.

theories.name: classical conditioning
theories.note: A theory in which an unconditioned stimulus triggers an unconditioned response and a conditioned stimulus triggers a conditioned response.

frameworks.name: stimulus–response model
frameworks.note: A model emphasizing the relation between stimulus and behavior rather than internal processes.

coined_terms.name: stress
coined_terms.note: Hans Selye introduced the term in a biological context and defined it as the non-specific response of the body to any demand.

coined_terms.name: hardiness
coined_terms.note: A term for the ability to be chronically stressed while remaining healthy.

concepts.name: homeostasis
concepts.note: The steady state that biochemical processes strive to maintain.

concepts.name: eustress
concepts.note: Enjoyable or inspiring stress with generally positive effects.

concepts.name: distress
concepts.note: Persistent unresolved stress that may lead to anxiety or withdrawal.

concepts.name: stress response
concepts.note: The body's physiological response to a stressor.

concepts.name: stressor
concepts.note: A stimulus or condition that produces stress.

principles.name: fight-or-flight response
principles.note: Sympathetic activation that prepares the body to fight or flee a threat.

principles.name: biological need for equilibrium
principles.note: Organisms strive to maintain or restore homeostasis.

theories.name: general adaptation syndrome
theories.note: Hans Selye's model of alarm, resistance, and exhaustion in response to stress.

frameworks.name: Holmes and Rahe Stress Scale
frameworks.note: An evaluation of different stresses in people's lives.

concepts.name: stress exposure training
concepts.note: Practicing important existing skills in stressful and distracting environments so they can be performed reliably.

concepts.name: stress
concepts.note: A process in which environmental demands are perceived to exceed resources.

principles.name: building confidence in the ability to perform under stress
principles.note: Training is effective when it produces a sense of mastery.

methods.name: skill development under benign conditions
methods.note: Practicing behavioral and cognitive skills that support performance under stress.

methods.name: provision of care and support
methods.note: Helping the subject form accurate expectations, reduce surprise, and plan.

concepts.name: stress management
concepts.note: Methods for coping with stress and improving overall well-being.

concepts.name: individual intervention
concepts.note: A workplace approach that begins by monitoring an individual's stressors.

methods.name: Autogenic training
methods.note: A listed stress-management technique.

methods.name: Cognitive therapy
methods.note: A listed psychotherapy for managing stress.

methods.name: Meditation
methods.note: A listed technique for coping with stress.

methods.name: Mindfulness
methods.note: A listed technique for coping with stress.

methods.name: Deep breathing
methods.note: A listed technique for reducing stress.

methods.name: Yoga Nidra
methods.note: A listed stress-management technique.

methods.name: Progressive relaxation
methods.note: A listed relaxation technique for managing stress.

methods.name: Time management
methods.note: A listed approach involving management of time to reduce stress.

concepts.name: sunk cost
concepts.note: A cost already incurred that cannot be recovered.

concepts.name: prospective cost
concepts.note: A future cost that may be avoided if action is taken.

concepts.name: sunk cost fallacy
concepts.note: Continuing an endeavor because money, effort, or time has already been invested.

axioms.name: only prospective costs are relevant to a rational decision
axioms.note: Classical economics and standard microeconomic theory treat future costs as relevant to rational decisions.

principles.name: bygones principle
principles.note: Past costs should not influence current decisions.

principles.name: marginal principle
principles.note: Decisions should depend on current alternatives and future consequences.

theories.name: standard microeconomic theory
theories.note: The theory that only prospective costs matter to rational decisions.

concepts.name: supercompensation
concepts.note: The post-training period in which a trained parameter has greater performance capacity than before training.

concepts.name: heterochronism of supercompensation
concepts.note: Different parameters require different recovery and adaptation times.

concepts.name: overtraining
concepts.note: A condition that may occur when the next workout takes place during recovery.

principles.name: supercompensation principle
principles.note: The body adapts after training by increasing fitness beyond its initial level.

theories.name: supercompensation theory
theories.note: A theory first put forth by Nikolai N. Yakovlev in 1949–1959 describing training, recovery, and increased fitness.

frameworks.name: four periods of training
frameworks.note: Initial fitness, training, recovery, and supercompensation.

frameworks.name: microcycles and macrocycles
frameworks.note: Training divisions in which microcycles develop basic parameters and macrocycles develop complex parameters.

concepts.name: Suum cuique
concepts.note: A Latin phrase commonly translated as “to each his own” or “may all get their due.”

concepts.name: justice
concepts.note: Plato's provisional definition is that everyone minds their own business and refrains from meddling in others' affairs.

principles.name: to each his own
principles.note: An old Greek principle of justice that each person should receive what is their own.

concepts.name: uncertainty
concepts.note: A situation involving imperfect or unknown information.

concepts.name: uncertainty-as-risk
concepts.note: Uncertainty designed into games, especially gambling, where chance is central.

concepts.name: Knightian uncertainty
concepts.note: A situation in which probabilities are unknown.

frameworks.name: uncertain database
frameworks.note: A computer-science model for storing and managing uncertain data.

frameworks.name: scenario optimization
frameworks.note: An optimization approach for situations where the user lacks full control over outcomes.

frameworks.name: stochastic optimization
frameworks.note: An optimization approach that represents uncertain outcomes.

concepts.name: value
concepts.note: The degree of importance of something or an action for determining what is best to do or how best to live.

concepts.name: ethical value
concepts.note: The degree of importance of something for determining the best action or life.

concepts.name: social value
concepts.note: The net social, environmental, and economic benefits of actions.

concepts.name: intrinsic value
concepts.note: Value possessed for its own sake rather than as a means.

concepts.name: instrumental value
concepts.note: Value possessed as a means toward something else that is good.

concepts.name: protected value
concepts.note: A value an individual is unwilling to trade off regardless of possible benefits.

theories.name: value theory
theories.note: The study of ethical value.

theories.name: value pluralism
theories.note: The view that several fundamental values may be equally correct yet conflict.

frameworks.name: value system
frameworks.note: A set of consistent values used for ethical or ideological integrity.

frameworks.name: idealized value system
frameworks.note: A value system without exceptions, codifiable as strict behavioral proscriptions.

frameworks.name: realized value system
frameworks.note: A value system containing exceptions to resolve practical contradictions.

concepts.name: vulnerability
concepts.note: The quality or state of being exposed to possible physical or emotional attack or harm.

concepts.name: social vulnerability
concepts.note: Vulnerability understood through the risks and assets of disadvantaged groups.

concepts.name: environmental vulnerability
concepts.note: The extent to which environmental changes can harm a system or community.

concepts.name: vulnerability research
concepts.note: A multidisciplinary field studying vulnerability, its measurement, and its assessment.

methods.name: measurement and assessment methods
methods.note: Methods being refined to measure and assess vulnerability.

frameworks.name: social and environmental vulnerability
frameworks.note: An approach analyzing the risks and assets of disadvantaged groups.

frameworks.name: Expert Working Group on Measuring Vulnerability
frameworks.note: A United Nations University forum bringing together vulnerability researchers.
